summary: A 1974 report on a protocol experiment run at BBN, when the TENEX line printer failed and the PDP-11 line printer was used over the ARPANET. It also served to study network protocols, based on the Cerf and Kahn design. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This experiment sent print data across the ARPANET while testing a protocol for reliable delivery. It reports how acknowledgments and retransmissions worked and describes a problem when the receiving computer restarted.

subtitle: A printer-sharing experiment used an ARPANET transfer to study reliable delivery between hosts.

tldr.problem: When BBN's main line printer failed, the team needed another way to print and also wanted to study network protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment used a window of unacknowledged bytes, sequence numbers and acknowledgments, with retransmission after a time-out and flags to establish an association.
tldr.outcome: A receiver restart caused duplicate printing, and the authors identify features not tested and recommend a larger sequence-number field.

today: RFC 700 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no replacement or update. It documents a 1974 experiment and distinguishes implemented features from proposed or untested ones.

sections.title: A Network Printer Experiment
sections.content:
In early February 1974, the main line printer on BBN's TENEX system failed. The authors used a PDP-11 printer over the ARPANET, both to obtain printed listings and to study network protocols.

The design was based on Cerf and Kahn's INWG Note #39. The RFC warns that not all features described in its protocol sketch had been implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: When their usual printer failed, the team sent work to another printer over the network. They used the job to test how reliably computers could exchange data.

sections.title: Windows, Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
The sender tracks a stream using LEFT and RIGHT pointers. Data before LEFT has been sent and acknowledged; data between LEFT and RIGHT has been sent but not yet confirmed. The low-order 16 bits of RIGHT are sent as a sequence number so the receiver can identify data even when messages arrive out of order.

The receiver stores data within its buffer area, discards out-of-range or bad-checksum messages, and passes continuous data at the left edge to the printer. Its acknowledgment identifies the next byte wanted and the available buffer space. If acknowledgments stop, a 10-second timeout causes the sender to retransmit the window. The receiver can also request retransmission of the full window using the "Say Again" flag.

Messages carried from 0 to 255 bytes of data and a one-byte checksum. The window size was fixed at 2048 bytes. The FRST flag marks the first message in an association, while HUH asks the sender to define the sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender tracks which bytes have been confirmed and resends data when confirmation stops. The receiver reports what byte it wants next and how much room it has.

sections.title: The Receiver-Restart Problem
sections.content:
When the PDP-11 receiver was reloaded while the sender was running, the first pages printed about six times. The sender repeatedly timed out and resent its window. The restarted receiver answered each message with HUH; the sender then marked the first message of each retransmission with FRST, causing the receiver to start printing the stream again.

The experimenters changed the receiver to ignore messages after sending HUH until it received FRST. They say this is not generally acceptable because losing either the HUH or the response can leave the receiver port unusable. They discuss another possible cure but note that it depends on a round-trip delay that may be impossible to define if messages can remain trapped indefinitely in network partitions.
sections.plainLanguage: After a receiver restart, repeated start markers made the same pages print again. The proposed quick fix could fail if a message was lost, so the report leaves the general solution open.

sections.title: Untested Features and Further Recommendations
sections.content:
The programs did not support changing the window size, reassembly, expanded internetwork addresses, multiple associations, or reliable creation and closing of associations. The window stayed at 2048 bytes.

The experiment used a one-byte checksum based on the low eight bits of the two's-complement negation of the sum of the other message bytes. The authors recommend a more reliable checksum. For rejecting a connection attempt, the report proposes REJECT, ABORT and ABNORMAL responses; during an association it proposes DONE and GAG release signals.
sections.plainLanguage: The report lists important features the experiment had not tried. It also recommends a stronger checksum and names signals for refusing or ending an association.

references.text: Cerf, V. and R. Kahn, INWG Note #39, the protocol design on which the experiment was based.
